title: The Opening
hook: the seven verses Muslims recite in every prayer (Quran 1)
tomorrow: a surah of three verses swears by time. what does it say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the restless mind: Arjuna's wind, and Krishna's two-handed answer. Practice and letting go. That closes the Gita. The next book begins with an opening.

A song through a neighbor's wall, a line a grandmother hummed: a sound can be familiar for years before its meaning is. Stand near a mosque at prayer time, or near a family praying at home, and you may hear seven short verses in Arabic, aloud or under the breath. Those verses answer yesterday's question: al-Fatiha, the Opening, the first surah of the Quran. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Bukhari's collection is plain about it: there is no prayer without the Opening of the Book.
screen: `A SOUND BEFORE A MEANING.` → `SEVEN SHORT VERSES.` → `NO PRAYER WITHOUT THE OPENING.`

segments.voice: Here's a story to hear it by. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that God said: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant, in two halves, and My servant will have what he asks. Then it goes verse by verse, like a call and an answer. The worshipper says, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds," and God says, My servant has praised Me. The worshipper names Him the Beneficent, the Merciful, and God says, My servant has extolled Me. Then the middle line: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. This, God says, is between Me and My servant. And the asking: "Show us the straight path." This is for My servant, and he shall have what he asked. So, in this hadith, al-Fatiha isn't only recited. It's a conversation, said in every prayer, with an answer to every line. And a detail to pass on: the Quran itself speaks of seven oft-repeated verses, and a hadith in Bukhari names them as this surah. A guest can listen for its shape: praise, then the turn to Thee alone, then the asking.
screen: `A PRAYER IN TWO HALVES.` · `PRAISE, AND AN ANSWER.` · `THEE ALONE.` · `SHOW US THE STRAIGHT PATH.` · then, large: `THE OPENING.`

segments.voice: Read one line slowly, aloud or under your breath: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." Then leave a long silence after it, the space where, in the hadith, an answer comes. If you pray, you can stay in that silence as prayer; if not, read it as a guest and simply listen to the quiet after the words.
Al-Fatiha: the Opening, seven verses, the first surah of the Quran, recited in every prayer.
Here's the line: the opening, a call with an answer at every verse. The Quran, one of seven.

howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in each of the daily prayers; in congregation the imam recites and those praying behind him listen or recite with him, depending on the school of law.

chat.says: a patient's mom prayed in our waiting room, same short arabic lines each time she stood. what is that?
options: Likely al-Fatiha, the Opening: seven verses said in every prayer, praise then asking.
Probably her own words for her kid; Muslims make up each prayer fresh, every time.
Likely the call to prayer; each person says it quietly to themselves before praying.
chat.meaning: Al-Fatiha is said in every prayer: praise, then 'Thee alone', then asking for the straight path. In a hadith, God answers each line.

tie.story: In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, God answers each line of al-Fatiha as the worshipper says it.
